# 4 Benchmarks (continued)

## SPLICED INDEXES {#a}

It is possible to change the index associated with the measurement of a specific portfolio over time, a good example being after a change in investment strategy. It is bad performance measurement practice to change the associated index retrospectively; therefore, a spliced index should be calculated to maintain the long-term return series of the associated benchmark. This can be achieved by chain-linking, or splicing, the respective indexes.

## MONEY-WEIGHTED BENCHMARKS (OR PUBLIC MARKET EQUIVALENTS) {#b}

All commercially produced indexes are time-weighted; there is no need to adjust for cash flow between time periods (although from time to time indexes are subject to corporate actions of various types that in effect generate cash flow). Money-weighted portfolio returns are impacted by cash flow, to ensure a like-for-like comparison a commercial index return can be recalculated to reflect the cash flow experience of the portfolio.

A type of money-weighted benchmark, the index comparison method (ICM) was first suggested by Long and Nickels. (Long and Nickels, "A Private Investment Benchmark" (1996).) First used internally in 1992, this method gradually gained acceptance as the Long-Nickels-Coller (LNC) method, then the Bannock-Long-Nickels-Coller (BLNC) method, and finally as the public market equivalent (PME) method. (Long, "The Common Mathematical Foundation of ACG's ICM and AICM and the K&S PME" (2008).)

The main disadvantage of money-weighted benchmarks is that the adjusted return is clearly different from the published index return and is unique to the cash flow experience of that portfolio. It makes the comparison of portfolio to public market equivalent return more accurate but does not aid the comparison against other asset managers with differing cash flow experience.
> **Note**
>
> In effect money-weighted benchmarks replicate the errors of money-weighted return calculations in the portfolio, but that does allow for an accurate one-on-one comparison.

## NORMAL PORTFOLIO {#c}

Commercial indexes may not adequately reflect the investment options open to individual portfolio managers. Normal portfolios provide an alternative benchmark consisting of specific securities available for investment (for example, the recommended list of securities from the in-house research team).

Although normal portfolios are a useful comparison against the real alternatives of the portfolio manager, they lack the stamp of independence required in the definition of a good benchmark.
